Thus, Zj and Zk are d-separated conditioning on Z[n]\{j,k}, which implies the conditional independence Zj ⊥ ⊥Zk | Z[n]\{j,k} based on the Markov assumption on (GZ, PZ;θ). Then we have {Zj, Zk} /∈ E(MZ). Proposition 2 (Moralized graph and Markov network). Given a causal DAG GZ and distribution PZ;θ with its Markov Network MZ, under Markov assumption, the undirected graph defined by MZ is the moralized graph of the true causal DAG GZ if and only if the SAF and SUCF assumptions are satisfied. Proof. We prove both directions as follows. Sufficient condition. We prove it by contradiction. Suppose that the structure defined by MZ is not equivalent to the moralized graph of GZ. Then, according to Lemma 1, there exists a pair of variables Zj and Zk, j ̸= k that are adjacent in the moralized graph but {Zj, Zk} /∈ E(MZ). Thus, we have Zj ⊥ ⊥Zk | Z[n]\{j,k}. Then we consider the following two cases: • If variables Zj and Zk correspond to a pair of neighbors in GZ, then they are adjacent. Together with the conditional independence relation Zj ⊥ ⊥Zk | Z[n]\{j,k}, this implies that the SAF assumption is violated. 20Causal Representation Learning from Multiple Distributions: A General Setting • If variables Zj and Zk correspond to a pair of non-adjacent spouses in GZ. Then they have an unshielded collider, indicating that the SUCF assumption is violated. Necessary condition. We prove it by contradiction. Suppose SUCF or SAF is violated, we have the following two cases: • Suppose SUCF is violated, i.e., there exists an unshielded collider Zj → Zi ← Zk in the DAG GZ such that Zj ⊥ ⊥Zk | Z[n]\{j,k}. This conditional independence relation indicates that {Zj, Zk} /∈ E(MZ). Since Zj and Zk are spouses, there exists an edge between them in the moralized graph of GZ, but is not contained in the structure defined by MZ, showing that they are not the same. • Suppose SAF is violated, i.e., there exists a pair of neighborsZj and Zk in the DAGGZ such that Zj ⊥ ⊥Zk | Z[n]\{j,k}. This conditional independence relation indicates that {Zj, Zk} /∈ E(MZ). Because Zj and Zk are adjacent in GZ, clearly they are also adjacent in the moralized graph of GZ. However, the edge between them is not contained in the structure defined by MZ, showing that they are not the same. Thus, when SUCF or SAF is violated, the structure defined by MZ is the moralized graph of the true DAG GZ. 21

llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: This paper addresses causal representation learning from multiple distributions in a general, completely nonparametric setting, without assuming parametric models on the data-generating process or the existence of hard interventions. The main contributions include proving that under sparsity constraints on the recovered graph over latent variables and suitable sufficient change conditions on causal influences, one can recover the moralized graph of the underlying Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) (Theorem 2). Furthermore, the recovered latent variables and their relations are shown to be connected to the true causal model in a specific, nontrivial way, where each latent variable is recovered as a function of itself and its 'intimate neighbors.' In some cases, most latent variables can be recovered up to component-wise transformations (Theorem 3, Remark 1). The paper also shows how the recovered moralized graph relates to the underlying causal graph under new relaxations of faithfulness assumptions (Proposition 2) and demonstrates the impossibility of finding independent components if the true latent causal DAG is not an empty graph (Corollary 1). Experimental results verify these theoretical claims.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The methodology involves learning a model (ˆg, ˆf, pˆZ, ˆΘ) from multiple distributions, assumed to originate from a nonlinear mixing function (g) of latent causal variables (Z) governed by a Structural Equation Model (SEM) with changing factors (θ). The core theoretical framework leverages the connection between pairwise conditional independence in a Markov network and cross-derivatives of the log-density. To recover latent variables and their causal structure, the method incorporates sparsity constraints on the estimated Markov network and relies on 'suitable sufficient change conditions' on causal influences. For practical implementation, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework is adopted, comprising a deep latent generative model (decoder) p(X|Z; ˆθ(u)) and a variational approximation (encoder) q(Z|X, u), minimizing the ELBO. Two prior distribution implementations are proposed: a nonparametric approach using normalizing flows to transform dependent latent variables into independent noise, and a parametric approach assuming a linear SEM with learnable scaling and bias parameters. An ℓ1 regularization on the estimated adjacency matrix (ˆA) is applied to encourage sparsity and learn the true causal structure.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The experimental validation is conducted on simulated data, providing access to the ground truth latent causal variables and structures. Two common causal structures are tested: a Y-structure (Z1→Z3←Z2, Z3→Z4) and a chain structure (Z1→Z2→Z3→Z4), each with 4 variables. The data generation process involves modular changes where noises are modulated by scaling and shifts sampled from uniform distributions (Unif[0.5, 2] and Unif[-2, 2], respectively), and scaling on Z is also sampled from Unif[0.5, 2]. The nonlinear mixing function 'g' is implemented using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) with orthogonal weights and LeakyReLU activations to ensure invertibility. Validation involves comparing recovered latent variables (ˆZ) against true latent variables (Z) using scatter plots and assessing the estimated causal adjacency matrix (ˆA) against the true causal graph, verifying one-to-one correspondences and the learned structure. Experiments are performed with both Laplace and Gaussian noise to demonstrate robustness.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The theoretical identifiability relies on several key assumptions: (A1) the probability density function of latent causal variables (pZ) must be twice continuously differentiable and positive; (A2) 'sufficient changes' in causal influences are required, necessitating a specific, potentially large number of distinct environments or domains (2n + |MZ| + 1 values of θ) to ensure linear independence of certain vectors. The theoretical results also depend on a 'sparsity constraint' on the recovered Markov network, which in practical implementation is approximated by an ℓ1 regularization on the estimated adjacency matrix (ˆA) due to difficulties in directly imposing a differentiable sparsity constraint on Markov network edges. The connection between the Markov network and the causal DAG relies on relaxed faithfulness assumptions (Single Adjacency-Faithfulness (SAF) and Single Unshielded-Collider-Faithfulness (SUCF)). While powerful, the method recovers latent variables 'up to specific, relatively minor indeterminacies,' meaning they are often a function of themselves and 'intimate neighbors,' not always a pure component-wise transformation. Furthermore, a permutation indeterminacy exists for the recovered latent variables.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work will explore scenarios where only a subset of the causal relations change, investigating how the underlying causal variables can be recovered under potentially weaker assumptions in such contexts. Additionally, a more sophisticated approach for imposing sparsity constraints on the Markov network, specifically by regularizing (I − ˆA)T Ω−1(I − ˆA) where Ω is a randomly sampled positive diagonal matrix, is left for future investigation as an alternative to the current ℓ1 regularization on the adjacency matrix.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Most existing methods that try to make image classifiers robust to spurious correlations (e.g., backgrounds, textures, co-occurring objects) require explicit group labels, human-annotated feature masks, or carefully curated environments.  This limits scalability and leaves models brittle when the correlation strength or the set of spurious factors changes at test time (contextual reliability).  The key challenge is therefore: "How can we automatically discover and neutralise spurious visual features – without any spurious-attribute annotations – while preserving or improving in-distribution accuracy?"  A solution would have high impact because it would remove the current annotation bottleneck and make robust training practical for large, constantly evolving image collections.
Methods: We propose Diffusion-based Counterfactual Debiasing (DCD), a training framework that pairs each real image with a set of automatically generated counterfactuals in which candidate spurious attributes are altered while the core class semantics are kept intact.  
1. Unsupervised spurious-factor mining
   a. Encode all training images with a frozen vision-language model (CLIP).
   b. Cluster CLIP embeddings within each class and compute difference vectors between cluster centroids.  Direction vectors that explain high intra-class variance but low inter-class variance are treated as candidate spurious directions.
   c. Rank directions by a "spuriousness score" = intra-class variance / inter-class variance.
2. Text-guided counterfactual generation
   a. For top-K directions we retrieve the nearest attribute words from the CLIP text vocabulary.
   b. Use a text-guided diffusion model (e.g. Stable Diffusion v2) with classifier-free guidance to edit each image: keep the original class prompt, replace / negate the attribute word, and run a few denoising steps (Plug-and-Play editing).
   c. Filter generated images by CLIP similarity to ensure the class identity is preserved.
3. Robust learning objective
   a. For every original–counterfactual pair (x,x′) enforce feature consistency: ‖fθ(x)−fθ(x′)‖².
   b. Add a contrastive loss that pushes apart features of different classes even after attribute editing.
   c. Combine with ERM loss on original images and a GroupDRO-style weight on hardest pairs; no group labels are needed – hardness is measured by the consistency loss.
   d. At test time we optionally ensemble predictions over T edited variants of the input (noise-stabilised).
Differences from prior work: (i) uses generative diffusion editing instead of hand-coded augmentations (SDA) or heuristic perturbations (MoCoDA); (ii) discovers spurious factors automatically from CLIP space, avoiding human annotation (ENP) or pre-defined groups (GroupDRO); (iii) pairs invariance loss with adaptive hard-pair reweighting, mitigating the robustness/accuracy trade-off noted in RSC-MDP and GC-DRO.
Experimental Setup: Datasets: Waterbirds, CelebA (Blond → Male), spurious-CIFAR (modified), MetaShift  "Dog on grass" subsets, and NICO++.  For more severe shifts we add our own Diff-Waterbirds test set where backgrounds are auto-replaced via diffusion.  
Baselines: ERM, Mixup, GroupDRO (clean & noisy groups), IRM, REx, GC-DRO, MoCoDA, ENP (with 10% annotated masks).  
Models: ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16 initialised with MoCo-v3 weights to follow the fair protocol of “Rethinking the Evaluation Protocol”.  Our encoder fθ shares the backbone; a two-layer projector is added for the consistency/contrastive losses.  
Metrics: (1) average accuracy, (2) worst-group accuracy (water vs. land, male vs. female, etc.), (3) accuracy drop under synthetic correlation reversal, (4) AUROC & FPR95 on NINCO to ensure OOD detection is not harmed, (5) label-noise robustness: repeat with 10% symmetric noise.  
Ablations: number of candidate directions K, quality filter threshold, use/not use ensemble at test time, replace diffusion edits with ordinary RandAug to isolate the benefit of counterfactuals.  All results averaged over 3 seeds.
Expected Result: • DCD improves worst-group accuracy by 6-12 pp over the best annotation-free baseline (MoCoDA) and matches or surpasses ENP even though ENP uses 10 % manual masks.
• In-distribution accuracy drops ≤1 pp compared to ERM, showing no severe trade-off.
• On Diff-Waterbirds, DCD retains >85 % of its ID accuracy, whereas ERM and IRM drop >20 pp.
• OOD detection AUROC on NINCO remains within 0.5 pp of the MoCo-v3 backbone, indicating that diffusion editing does not impair feature space quality.
• Under 10 % label noise DCD’s accuracy degrades <3 pp vs. >8 pp for GroupDRO, confirming implicit noise robustness.
Expected Conclusion: The proposed Diffusion-based Counterfactual Debiasing demonstrates that large text-guided generative models can be harnessed as fully automatic providers of causal counterfactuals, eliminating the need for spurious-attribute annotations and outperforming existing robustness techniques.  Academically, the work unifies ideas from causal representation learning, diffusion-based image editing, and distributional robustness, opening a new avenue for "generative intervention" research.  Practically, it provides a scalable recipe: given only class labels and off-the-shelf generative models, practitioners can harden image classifiers against unforeseen distribution shifts.  Future extensions include applying the same pipeline to video and multimodal tasks and exploring tighter integration with causal discovery modules to refine the attribute direction ranking.
